exact-consumer-identity.text: A relying contract wants Alice's eligible checkpoint in one chosen registry. A valid checkpoint elsewhere must not authorize its payment. The reviewed model makes that choice explicit before it examines a candidate holding.

identity-and-authority.text: The model binds to the public Singular revision d69ab005c3b710aeebf033d3c5cd08c56feb5643. It imports the actual application-held identity declarations from that same pinned tree. This nested model coexists with Singular's reduced economic model; importing it does not establish a production implementation.

stateAsset returns the release's state policy and the hash of the encoded State preimage containing the creation seed. activeAsset uses that full registry asset and the encoded AID key in its Active preimage. The active asset's policy is the registry's policy. These are the imported functions, not a second naming algorithm copied into KERI.

The checkpoint validator recognises a checkpoint the same way: the spent input holds exactly one representative asset, the active asset of the validator's registry and the datum's identifier, and every successor holds that asset again; no arm of the validator mints or burns it.

The consumer definitions live in CardanoKeri.ConsumerIdentity; their exact source identities and theorem statements are recorded in the repository's consumer bindings and theorem-story ledger. The preserved custody baseline is KERI revision ff78b1c0d87a29d2f856cb32f1261591f84831db. All existing lifecycle eligibility, custody and economic contracts remain in force. The new holding predicate adds identity and observation requirements.

the-bounded-registration-bridge.text: The connected model begins at actual genesis and executes both folds. It never starts by declaring that a final holding is valid.

createRegistry checks configuration correspondence and actual imported genesis. registerJoint executes booking, the preserved economic fold, the full-identity fold and Checkpoint registration. It checks the selected outputs' key, reference, credential, datum, quantity, deposit and trie mapping, then constructs the stored registration origin.

moneyAgreementB compares complete spent references, input reference/value pairs, ordered output amounts, fee, donation and validity interval between the two fold observations. The bridge also requires the registry's deposit to be the checkpoint's deposit plus freeze bond, and the declared carrier to be exactly the lovelace the registered checkpoint holds, so the initial pool is what the carrier holds above the minimum ADA, the deposit and the freeze bond (see the checkpoint output's value).

The proofs establish inversion, completeness under the explicit component premises, delivered-origin correspondence and preservation of the old eligibility predicate. The connected fixture continues through all four rotation branches, freeze and recovery, poison and clearing, concrete conviction, booking and matching completion. It executes a full-identity terminal fold against the same state reference and money observations. A valid foreign request cannot complete the stored pending request; a mixed fold that consumes that request can.

what-the-interpretation-must-establish.text: The model takes a codec, hash, AID-to-key function and release-indexed datum decoder as interpretation inputs. Its finite separation theorems expose the codec and collision premises in their types. Distinct AID labels do not imply distinct encoded keys without a corresponding mapping premise.

The executable corpus publishes its finite preimage tables and checks every pair in the declared domain. Constant codecs, constant hashes and a constant reduced-registry map fail their respective premises. These controls use a fixture codec and hash; the concrete bytes follow in the next section.

realizesState checks the credential, representative quantity, decoded AID and datum facts, and the output's lovelace: the decoded state is compared with the intended state, both with the pool set to zero, because the pool is an amount held in the value and not a fact in the datum; the lovelace must be exactly what the intended state holds. It has no current-reference or unspentness check. Local fixture observations are explicitly selected model interpretations, not a production observer. No checkpoint expiry or renewal behavior is supplied by the model.

the-concrete-bytes.text: The model declares one concrete interpretation in CardanoKeri.ConsumerIdentity.Bytes. The registry key of an AID is the AID's qualified CESR text bytes. The codec is the Plutus Data serialisation of the Preimage type in Singular's singular_state/preimage module at the pinned revision. The hash is BLAKE2b-256, as in that module. The datum decoder is declared in the checkpoint datum.

The upstream model carries byte strings such as transaction ids, policies, asset names and keys as natural numbers. Each such field carries its bytes through a bijective base-256 numeral, so empty strings and leading zero bytes keep their identity. Output indices and deposits are plain integers.

A 256-bit digest of inputs of any length cannot be injective, so no proof of collision freedom exists; the statements name the assumption in their types. With it, the theorems for different AIDs, different seeds and a rival seed's registry hold for the concrete bytes.

The vector table lists, for each state policy, seed and AID, the key, both serialised preimages, both names and the representative asset a genuine holding carries. The Lean emits the table and checks the committed copy. Each row runs the consumer predicate: the committed asset is accepted, and a changed state policy, transaction id, output index, AID or asset name is refused. Changing any committed field of the table fails the check. The same code reproduces every preimage and name of Singular's own table at the pinned revision, across its five roles.

These checks cover the listed inputs only. The registration approval role splices an already serialised holding address and is outside the consumer statements. The Aiken consumer predicate reproduces the table, as described in the concrete identity bytes in Aiken.

the-checkpoint-datum.text: A contract author holds a candidate checkpoint output with an inline datum. The consumer must read that datum exactly as the checkpoint writes it: which AID it belongs to, whether it is live or awaiting termination, whether it is poisoned, whether its bond is frozen and when it was born. A datum that does not have that shape is refused. The model declares this datum, version 2, in CardanoKeri.CheckpointDatum, together with the decoder the consumer runs.

Version 1, constructor 0, is the layout the checkpoint validator writes today. It carries keys, thresholds, witnesses and counters, but no poison, no freeze, no birth slot and no pending-termination form, so a poisoned checkpoint and a clean one would be byte-identical. The decoder refuses it. Version 2 is written by the model first; the on-chain validator adopts it later.

The key material is constructor 0 with six fields, in the version 1 types: current keys (a list of byte strings), current threshold, next keys, next threshold, witnesses (a list of byte strings) and toad (an integer). A threshold is constructor 0 over an integer (unweighted) or constructor 1 over a list of clauses, each a list of weights; a weight is constructor 0 over a numerator and a denominator. A Boolean is Aiken's: false is constructor 0 and true is constructor 1, both without fields.

The serialisation is Plutus Data's: constructors 0 to 6 as tags 121 to 127, 7 to 127 as tags 1280 to 1400, any other index as tag 102 over the index and the fields; non-empty lists indefinite; maps definite; byte strings definite up to 64 bytes, otherwise in chunks of 64; integers plain below 2^64, otherwise tagged big numbers. A raw application datum is these bytes carried through the same bijective numeral as the identity bytes. The reader also accepts the other well-formed encodings of the same Data. One layout serves every release at this model revision; a new layout is a new version constructor.
What the Lean proves about it:
Reading back: every Data, read from its serialisation with any rest, returns with that rest (parse_cbor), and every serialised element is a byte, so the raw carrier is faithful (decode_raw).
Written datums decode: for every AID, key material and state with an output, the decoder returns that AID and the state's facts (decodeData_datum, decode_written).

Nothing else decodes: an accepted Data is exactly a written datum (decodeData_complete). A wrong version, version 1 included, a wrong number of fields, an unknown form and a field of the wrong kind are each refused (wrong_version_refused, version_one_refused, version_arity_refused, unknown_form_refused, live_arity_refused, pending_arity_refused, live_fields_typed, pending_fields_typed).
The decoder is a function of the raw datum alone: one datum, one result, under every release (decode_deterministic, decode_release_independent).

The consumer: with this decoder in the concrete interpretation, a holding carrying the datum written for any state, funded pools included, is accepted exactly when that state is consumable (written_holding_iff). A funded registration passes the registration bridge's datum check (funded_registration_agrees), and a version 1 datum is refused (version_one_holding_refused).

The twenty-six consumer statements are proved for every interpretation, so they hold with this one. Their wording is unchanged; the three that compare a decoded state with an intended one, through realizesState and the registration bridge, compare the datum's facts and the output's lovelace, so they apply to funded registrations too.

The vector table lean/checkpoint-datum-vectors.json lists seven written datums with the decoder's result and the consumer's verdict on a genuine holding (registered and funded, juvenile, rotated with weighted thresholds and witnesses, poisoned, frozen, pending termination, numbers beyond 2^64), and twenty-nine datums the decoder refuses, each a named change: version 1, an unknown version, every wrong arity, every field of the wrong kind, a trailing byte, a truncated datum. The Lean emits the table and checks the committed copy against the decoder and the consumer predicate. Changing any committed field fails the check, and every node of every accepted datum, replaced by a node of another kind, is refused.

These checks cover the listed inputs; the theorems cover all inputs. The Aiken consumer decodes version 2 (the datum decoder in Aiken); the on-chain validator does not write version 2 yet. Reading the pool and the bonds from the value is modelled in the checkpoint output's value. This code is not for mainnet.

The correspondence between the Haskell library and this model is stated over datums the ledger admits: the model accepts one unbroken 65-byte string that the ledger and the library refuse (see entry 16 of the Lean correspondence register).

the-checkpoint-outputs-value.text: A contract author holds a candidate checkpoint output and has read its datum. The datum says the checkpoint is live and its bond is not frozen, but it carries no amounts. The author wants to know the bonds are really there: the output's lovelace must be what that state holds, and a holding missing part of a bond must be refused. The model states this amount in CardanoKeri.CheckpointValue as State.heldValue.

The diagram reads in words: a registration delivers the minimum ADA, the deposit, the freeze bond and the initial pool the registrant chooses. Every later step moves exactly the amounts its flow names. A freeze pays the freeze bond to the hunter, a rotation with a deposit brings it back, and a conviction pays the deposit to the convictor and the bond and pool to the refund address. The pending output keeps only the minimum ADA, which the termination booking consumes.

Here Mc is the registry's minimum ADA, D the deposit and B the freeze bond of the checkpoint's parameters, and pool the premium pool. The datum's facts and the lovelace together give back the whole state: the pool is the lovelace above the floor (withValue_iff, realizes_determines_state).

Every step keeps the amounts: what the input holds plus what the step takes in equals what the output holds plus what it pays out (held_amounts_conserved, held_value_conserved); a registration holds the minimum ADA plus everything it takes in (registration_holds_carrier).

A conviction pays out everything the live checkpoint held except the minimum ADA, and the pending output holds exactly the minimum ADA the termination booking requires (conviction_pays_out_every_amount, pending_holds_minimum_ada).
A holding below the floor realizes no state with those facts, whatever its pool (short_holding_refused, missing_bond_lovelace_refused).

The registry books a carrier of at least Mc + D_registry, where the registry's deposit is the checkpoint's deposit plus freeze bond; one lovelace short is refused (short_carrier_registration_refused). A successful joint registration delivers exactly Mc + D + B + pool0 (registerJoint_value).

The vector table lean/checkpoint-value-vectors.json takes the seven states of the datum vectors and gives, for each, the lovelace its output holds, its floor and what a holding with those datum facts reads as at lovelace values around them: the state itself only at the lovelace it holds. It also books registration carriers with initial pools of 0, 3 and five million, refuses one carrier short by one lovelace, and records the connected registration fixture, whose carrier of 17 is the minimum ADA 4, the deposit 8, the freeze bond 2 and the pool 3. The Lean emits the table and checks the committed copy; changing any committed field fails the check.

These checks cover the listed inputs; the theorems cover all inputs. The consumer predicate itself does not read the value: a relying contract that needs the bonds checks the lovelace against the floor, and the validator that enforces the amounts on chain is the datum version 2 work (#339). How an honest owner recovers the deposit, the freeze bond or the pool is not settled by the model.

the-consumer-predicate-in-aiken.text: onchain/lib/cardano_keri/consumer.ak is consumableHoldingB clause for clause, in the Lean order: authenticated network, complete release and checkpoint credential, the holding at the checkpoint validator's address (its credential with no stake credential, not the application's), a total quantity of one for the representative asset, and a decoded datum for the intended AID in a consumable state (present, unfrozen, unpoisoned, at least W old). The registry and representative asset names follow registryAsset and representativeAsset. The network, release, checkpoint credential, seed and AID are arguments fixed by the relying contract; the environment carries the credential the integration resolved, and an unresolved one refuses. The hash, codec, AID-to-key map and datum decoder are four function arguments (Aiken data types cannot hold functions, so the Lean's Interpretation record becomes those four arguments); the candidate output selects none of them.

Two executable layers check it. All 35 queries of simulator/consumer-corpus.json are generated by scripts/consumer-vectors.mjs into consumer_corpus_vectors.ak, one test per row carrying the row's own expected result; the four rows whose interpretation tables are incomplete or ambiguous require the predicate to fail, never to answer. Property tests (consumer_tests.ak) run each clause beside its refusal over generated variations and name the theorem they mirror (CI01 to CI16). The vectors are regenerated and compared by node scripts/consumer-vectors.mjs --check.

the-connected-example.text: consumer_identity_example is a spending validator for a relying contract. It is parameterised by the consumer context (network, release, checkpoint credential, seed, AID) and the checkpoint parameters, and it spends only if some reference input is a consumable holding for that context, on the concrete identity bytes and the datum decoder of the Lean model. The end-to-end specification (ConsumerE2ESpec) runs it on a local test chain against the checkpoints the production validators delivered. The consumer's context (network, application policy and credential, state program and policy, seed, the AID as its qualified CESR text, the checkpoint credential) is taken from the registry environment of the devnet, not declared. The maturity window W is the relying contract's own choice (Lean T9_juvenility_is_consumer_only: no transition of the registry reads it); the test uses 30 seconds. A spend that references a holding settles, or is rejected when the consumer script evaluates false, as the Lean predicate says of the output the chain holds:

After the terminating fold no output at the checkpoint validator holds the token, so the consumer has nothing to reference. Each refusal carries no other script and passes the ledger rules, so the rejection is the consumer's own verdict; each reading also checks that the story and the Lean predicate evaluated over the output the chain holds name the same failing clauses, and that the node settles the spend exactly when none fails. The datums are the ones the validators wrote, version 2, the AID as its qualified CESR text.

The Lean writes no datum for an absent or a convicted state (CheckpointDatum.datum is none for both), so a retired holding with a version 2 datum does not exist; those two arms of consumable_state stay covered by the Aiken predicate tests.

Seeded fixture cases. Three cases are not reachable by any registry transaction on main and stay seeded: a poisoned checkpoint (no transaction writes the poison flag), a holding carrying a version 1 datum (the checkpoint datum has no such form), and a holding carrying the representative token twice (the registry mints it once). A test-only policy mints them at a test checkpoint credential. They prove the consumer's decoder and quantity clauses over those bytes and say nothing of a registration journey.
One registry. The refusal of another registry's holding is shown by a consumer that fixes another seed and reads the genuine holding; a holding of a second, honestly created registry is not built.

Declared limits of the example. A script cannot observe the network or resolve a release, so the example's environment is the context it is parameterised with (the trusted integration's observation). now is the lower bound of the transaction's validity interval, in the same unit as the datum's birth time and the maturity parameter; a transaction with no finite lower bound is refused. A datum the decoder does not accept makes the consumer refuse the holding; it never makes the script fail. The pool and the bond amounts are held in the output's value and are not read from it (the datum decodes with a pool of 0; #339). The datum a holding carries is read from the chain; no check ties it to the registration record that produced it (#514).

the-concrete-identity-bytes-in-aiken.text: The concrete identity bytes in Aiken.

onchain/lib/cardano_keri/consumer_identity_bytes.ak computes, in Aiken, the names the Lean concrete interpretation computes. It is plugged into the predicate through the existing function arguments; the predicate is unchanged.

The relying contract fixes the state policy, the seed and the AID. The AID is the Lean aidOfCesr of its CESR text: the bijective base-256 number of the text's UTF-8 bytes. Only the State and Active preimages are computed, because the predicate uses only those two roles.

The Lean vectors. consumer_identity_vectors.ak is generated by scripts/consumer-identity-vectors.mjs from lean/consumer-identity-vectors.json (just gen-consumer-identity-vectors). just check-consumer-identity-vectors rejects any drift and runs in the Onchain CI job beside the corpus vectors check. For each of the eight vectors there is one test per claim: the state preimage, the registry name, the key (and the AID back from the key), the active preimage, the active name and the representative asset, each compared with the Lean bytes.

Properties (consumer_identity_tests.ak): the byte carrier laws, every width of the output index, the change of the active name under each committed field (seed transaction id, seed output index, state policy, AID) over a grid of seventy-two contexts, and the predicate itself accepting the holding named by the concrete bytes and refusing every rival's.

Connected. ConsumerE2ESpec recomputes the names from the Lean layout, checks them against the vectors, and on the local test chain settles a spend that references the genuine holding so named and refuses, in the consumer script, a spend that references it with another credential or another seed fixed, and the frozen and the pending-termination checkpoints.

What stays a declared test choice: the environment (the contract's own context stands for the trusted integration's observation) and the three seeded fixture cases above. These checks cover the vectors and the generated variations only: byte strings of more than 64 bytes would be serialised in chunks, which no vector reaches (a CESR text is 44 bytes). This code is not for mainnet.

the-datum-decoder-in-aiken.text: onchain/lib/cardano_keri/consumer_checkpoint_datum.ak is CardanoKeri.CheckpointDatum.decodeData and decode over the inline datum as Plutus data, with the Lean's field readers under the same names. The consumer validator passes the concrete identity bytes and this decoder to the predicate.

Raw bytes are the ledger's. The Lean reads the datum's serialised bytes. On chain the ledger delivers the inline datum to the script already as plutus data, so the Aiken decoder starts at the data and has no counterpart of parse. This is a representation boundary, declared here: nothing in this repository runs the ledger's parse, and the connected test above is the only evidence that the data the ledger delivers is the data the Lean describes. In the Aiken tests, aiken/cbor.deserialise of a vector's datum bytes stands in for the ledger's parse; bytes that are not one whole datum never reach the decoder, as the Lean's ofBytes? refuses them. The one vector with tagged big numbers (large-numbers) cannot be read that way, because that function stops the whole test run on a tagged big number. Its tests use data the generator builds, and require that this data serialises, with the plutus serialiser, to the vector's bytes, so the bytes of that row are checked against the Lean's inside the suite.

The decoder never fails. Every unwrap of plutus data follows a test of its kind, so a datum the decoder does not accept is None, never an abort: a contract that scans reference inputs skips an unrelated output's datum instead of failing on it.
Two executable layers check it, beside the connected run.

The Lean vectors. consumer_checkpoint_datum_vectors.ak is generated by scripts/checkpoint-datum-vectors.mjs from lean/checkpoint-datum-vectors.json (just gen-checkpoint-datum-vectors). Each of the thirty-six rows has a test that the decoder returns the row's result and a test that the consumer predicate, on the concrete identity bytes and this decoder, returns the row's verdict; each test is named after the row. The Lean CI job runs node scripts/checkpoint-datum-vectors.mjs --check as the last step of scripts/check-consumer-design.sh and fails on any drift; just check-checkpoint-datum-vectors runs the same check locally.

Properties (consumer_checkpoint_datum_tests.ak): the decoder never fails on arbitrary data; every value of each field it reads decodes to the Lean's result; and every other kind of node in each position, including each component of the key material, is refused.
These checks cover the vectors and the generated variations only. This code is not for mainnet.

what-a-reader-answers-about-an-identifie.text: What a reader answers about an identifier.

A relying party asks a reader about Alice's identifier at a stated chain point. It wants one of five answers: active, pending termination, terminal, never registered or unavailable. A convicted identity must never look like an unknown one, and a failed read must never look like an absence. The consumer predicate above judges one output; CardanoKeri.ReaderStatus states the answer about the identifier.

The reader fixes the same context as the consumer: network, release, registry seed, identifier and checkpoint credential. For the chain point it answers at it holds the resolved environment and two observations. The first is every unspent output that holds the identifier's representative asset. The second is the history of the registry: the changes of every fold, in order, from the registry's creation through the point. Of each change the reader keeps the key it registers or the key it terminates. Each observation names the chain point and the asset, or the registry, it is about; one made at another point, or about another asset or registry, establishes nothing for this question. The one exception, described below, is a history that refutes itself. An observation that is absent, stale, failed or incomplete is not established. The model has no clock: it compares chain points for equality only, and holds no lag, no age and no number of slots. How fresh a read must be is a setting of each deployment.

The leaf of the identifier's key is not observed. It is replayed from the history. The registry starts with no member. Each fold's changes are applied in order: a registration binds a key the registry does not know as active, and a termination makes an active key terminal. After a replay that succeeds the key reads unknown exactly when no change of any fold names it, and terminal exactly when some fold terminates it (replayed_leaf). Only a complete history establishes a leaf. A history that starts late or misses a fold establishes none.

A history can refute itself. It does when no registry before the supplied folds makes them replay. For a history that says it is complete the registry before is the empty one. For an incomplete history it is any registry, because the folds the reader misses may have made any change. A fold with no change, or a key registered twice, terminated twice or registered after its termination, fails its replay from every registry, so no missing fold explains it (unreplayable_iff). A history that says it is complete and starts with a termination fails from the empty registry. Such a history is the history of no registry. Beside it the answer is unavailable whatever the holders show, complete or not, and whatever chain point and registry it names (broken_history_unavailable).

A history of the identifier's registry through the asked point can also contradict a holder. It does when no registry before its folds makes them replay and leave the identifier's key active. Beyond a history that refutes itself, that is a complete history whose replayed leaf is not active (leaf_allows_holder_iff), or an incomplete history that holds the termination of the identifier's key (incomplete_admits_active_iff). On a reachable history of the registry, under the two identity assumptions of this page, a key that is not active has no holder (holders_follow_leaf), so the two observations cannot both be true of one chain. The answer is unavailable (holder_against_history_unavailable, incomplete_history_refusing_unavailable).

An honest history does neither. Take a history that replays from the registry's creation, and an observation that holds some of its folds, in order, and all of them when it says it is complete. Some registry, the empty one when the observation says it is complete, makes the observed folds replay, so the observation does not refute itself (honest_history_does_not_refute_itself). That registry need not be the one the real registry was before the first observed fold: when a fold is missing in the middle, the replay succeeds from a registry that already holds what the missing fold did. The model does not rebuild the earlier registry from a partial history; it asks only whether one could exist. When the full history leaves the identifier's key active, an incomplete observation of some of its folds admits that key and does not refuse a holder (part_of_history_admits_active, honest_partial_history_allows_holder). An incomplete history that does not refuse the holder gives the answer the reader gives with no history at all (incomplete_history_is_a_gap). A history about another point or another registry that does not refute itself establishes nothing for this question (history_not_established).

One observation suffices. In an authenticated context a recognised holder decides active or pending termination when the history is missing, or is incomplete and does not refuse it, and a complete history decides terminal or never registered when the holders are not established. Each rests on a statement about a reachable history of the registry, under the two identity assumptions of this page. If the holders the reader lists are every holder, an answer of active or pending termination means the key's leaf is active and the holder named is the only one, whatever the history observation holds (holder_decides_alone). If a complete history the reader holds is the registry's own folds, an answer of terminal or never registered means the leaf is as answered and no output holds the asset, whatever the holding observation holds (history_decides_alone). A gap in the observation an answer does not need does not make the answer unavailable.

The diagram shows the whole decision for an authenticated context. The reader reads who holds the asset and what the history says. Each status has one path, and every other combination, an unauthenticated context included, ends in unavailable.
Each status has one observation that decides it and one that must not contradict it.

Every evidence value gets exactly one of the five answers (exactly_one_answer), and the executable classifier is the relation (classify_iff_answers). The four statuses are each characterised in both directions (active_iff, pendingTermination_iff, terminal_iff, neverRegistered_iff).

Pending termination covers both stages after a conviction. Before the termination is booked the holder is the convicted checkpoint; after it, the termination request at the application's credential, which carries no datum. The answer names the holder, and the custody it read says which of the two it is (pending_termination_custody). In the checkpoint system the identifier's state is pending termination on both sides of the booking. On evidence that realizes a reachable system, with an authenticated context and both observations established, the reader answers pending termination on both sides, and after the booking the holder it names is the request the booking placed: its reference is the one the system records for the pending termination (booked_termination_is_pending).

Eligibility is not a status. The consumer predicate decides it for one output. In an authenticated context a live checkpoint of the identifier is accepted exactly when it is not frozen, not poisoned and old enough (active_holder_eligibility), so a young, a frozen and a poisoned checkpoint are each an active identity the consumer refuses. An output the consumer accepts is answered active when the evidence establishes it as the one holder and the history does not refuse it (eligible_holder_is_active); beside a history that refuses it the same output is answered unavailable (holder_against_history_unavailable). When the answer is pending termination or terminal, the consumer refuses every holder the evidence establishes (pending_or_terminal_holder_refused). On a reachable history of the registry, under the two identity assumptions, a chain state that warrants pending termination or terminal has no unspent output the consumer accepts, in any environment and at any time (pending_or_terminal_never_consumable).

A missing token decides nothing. When no output holds the asset and no leaf is established, the answer is unavailable (missing_token_alone_unavailable). The registry's history shows why: on a reachable history, under the two identity assumptions, the asset has exactly one holder while the leaf is active and none under every other leaf (holders_follow_leaf), so an identifier that was never registered and one that is terminal look the same to a reader that only counts tokens. The connected lifecycle example has both: at the registry's creation identifier 11 has no fold, and after its conviction, booking and terminating fold its history registers and terminates its key; neither has a holder, and only the history tells them apart (missing_token_fits_two_lifecycles).

Terminal comes from the history alone. The evidence has no place for an observed burn, so a burn cannot be read as a termination. The registry's history gives the reason the replay is enough: on a reachable history, under the two identity assumptions, a transaction that burns the identifier's asset is a fold of its registry that terminates its key and leaves the leaf terminal (burn_is_the_terminating_fold). The burn of another registry's asset, or of another key's, is a burn of another asset.

The replay is the registry's own rule. Along a history of the public registry model, replaying a registry's folds from no member gives exactly that registry's members (registry_members_are_replayed), because the replay of an accepted fold is the fold's own effect (applyFold_of_accepted). So when a complete history the reader holds of the registry through the point is the registry's own folds, the leaf it replays is the registry's leaf (replayed_leaf_is_registry_leaf), and such a history always establishes it (complete_history_establishes_the_leaf).

The answer is stated against the two models of the system. The first is the public registry's history, with its complete unspent set and every registry's members. Evidence is faithful to it (Faithful) when the holders it lists are every holder and a complete history it holds of the registry through the point is the registry's own folds; nothing is asked of an incomplete history. On faithful evidence a status the reader gives is one the state of the identifier's registry in that history warrants (status_is_warranted). In the other direction, on a reachable history with an authenticated context, faithful evidence that establishes both the holders and a leaf gets the status the state warrants (warranted_status_is_answered), and the four statuses exclude one another (warrants_exclusive). These two statements rest on the two identity assumptions of this page, a faithful finite encoding and collision freedom, taken over the preimages the history holds and the identifier's active preimage. Without them two keys could share an asset name, and a holder would say nothing about a leaf.

The second model is the checkpoint system, with the lifecycle state of every identifier. On evidence that realizes a reachable system (Realizes), an answer other than unavailable is the status of the identifier's state: never registered for absent, active for live, pending termination for pending termination, terminal for convicted (status_follows_lifecycle). When the context is also authenticated and the evidence establishes both the holders and a leaf, the answer is that status (lifecycle_status_is_answered). Evidence that establishes neither observation realizes every system and is answered unavailable.

lean/reader-status-vectors.json carries 72 rows on the concrete identity bytes and the version 2 datum: for each, the evidence, the status, the custody read, the leaf replayed, whether the history admits a holder, the holder named and the consumer's verdict on it. Twenty-three rows end in a status and forty-nine in unavailable. Six of the twenty-three answer from the holder beside a history that is not complete. Nineteen of the forty-nine hold a history that refuses a holder and establishes no leaf: seven complete ones that fail their replay, two of them beside a holder; nine incomplete ones, eight of them beside a holder, of which two hold the termination of the identifier's key and the others are histories no registry could have; and three that refute themselves and name another point or another registry. ReaderStatusDriver.lean --check recomputes every row from its own committed evidence and requires every changed field to fail; --run answers one scenario read from standard input. Fifty-six single-site changes of the classifier and of the replay are each detected by the row bound to them (lean/retained-parking/reader-status-mutants.json). These are model checks. A reader implementation needs its own two layers of tests against these vectors and against a chain.

evidence-and-implementation-acceptance.text: The source includes twenty-six proved consumer statements with bound Given/When/Then stories. The model driver emits the complete accepted and refused queries, connected certificate events and actual fold observations. The browser and command-line simulator use the same pure consumer function; their replay gates compare those observations with freshly generated Lean output. Mutation controls change executable decision sites and retain setup failures separately from detected behavioral faults.

This establishes a local model and simulator candidate. Independent acceptance, hosted checks and publication are separate evidence. Production completion under the consumer implementation ticket requires both real implementation properties and connected ledger-boundary tests, including the observation obligations above. Neither layer is supplied by proving the model or replaying its corpus. This code is not for mainnet.
